title: Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents

paper.title: Reward-rate Policy Gradient for Efficient Machine Learning Engineering Agents
paper.abstract:
Abstract Traditional reinforcement learning (RL) techniques focus on maximizing expected cumulative reward, where each action assumes to take a constant unit of time.
However, this assumption does not hold for agentic RL tasks such as machine learning engineering (MLE) agents, where actions involve data loading, feature engineering, and model training that take variable durations.
Efficiency matters in modern agentic RL where actions are costly.
To address this limitation, we adapt from continuous-time RL and Semi-Markov Decision Process (SMDP) formulation and propose Reward-rate Policy Gradient (RPG) , where we focus on optimizing the reward rate — the long-term reward per unit of time. RPG estimates the reward rate from off-policy samples, then charges each action for the time it consumes at that rate.
We first conduct theoretical analysis in the bandit setting to establish that RPG approximates the optimal reward rate and empirically demonstrate it outperforms baselines while avoiding enumeration over the policy space, a known issue for an existing method.
We then further apply RPG on a small language model (Qwen3.5-4B) with self-improvement loops and empirically show it obtains higher rewards within a fixed time budget than vanilla RL on MLE-Bench and NanoGPT, with a 19.2% and 85.7% margin, respectively.
Our method provides a practical solution for optimizing performance under wait time considerations in modern agentic RL tasks, where actions interact with external environments and cost time.

However, this assumption does not hold for agentic RL tasks such as machine learning engineering (MLE) agents, where actions involve data loading, feature engineering, and model training that take variable durations. Efficiency matters in modern agentic RL where actions are costly. To address this limitation, we adapt from continuous-time RL and Semi-Markov Decision Process (SMDP) formulation and propose Reward-rate Policy Gradient (RPG) , where we focus on optimizing the reward rate — the long-term reward per unit of time. RPG estimates the reward rate from off-policy samples, then charges each action for the time it consumes at that rate. We first conduct theoretical analysis in the bandit setting to establish that RPG approximates the optimal reward rate and empirically demonstrate it outperforms baselines while avoiding enumeration over the policy space, a known issue for an existing method. We then further apply RPG on a small language model (Qwen3.5-4B) with self-improvement loops and empirically show it obtains higher rewards within a fixed time budget than vanilla RL on MLE-Bench and NanoGPT, with a 19.2% and 85.7% margin, respectively. Our method provides a practical solution for optimizing performance under wait time considerations in modern agentic RL tasks, where actions interact with external environments and cost time. † † footnotetext: Website: https://muhang-tian.com/reward-rate/ Code: https://github.com/MuhangTian/Reward-rate-Policy-Gradient 1 Introduction RL has been used extensively to train language models (LMs) and agents, where the standard approach is to maximize expected cumulative reward ( Christiano et al., 2017 ; Zhang et al., 2025a ) . Recently, there has been interest in MLE agents, where the goal is to automate the MLE pipeline to achieve best performance on held-out data ( Chan et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2025 ; Nam et al., 2026 ) . Current approaches mostly apply a strong LM in a search procedure: AIDE explores the space of candidate programs as a tree ( Jiang et al., 2025 ) , while MLE-STAR retrieves an initial solution with a search engine and then refines its targeted components ( Nam et al., 2026 ) . A separate line trains the model itself with RL on performance score ( Yang et al., 2025 ) . However, none of these methods perform gradient updates that fundamentally change agents’ behavior to learn to generate more efficient solutions. In MLE , each action takes variable time and resources, so it is important to consider samples’ costs for practicality — we want agents that are not only good, but also efficient . One solution is to use multi-objective RL and search for the Pareto frontier between performance and time ( Roijers et al., 2013 ; Hayes et al., 2022 ) , but computing the set of optimal solutions is often infeasible and compute-heavy ( Hayes et al., 2022 ) . These limitations motivate an objective that intrinsically aims for long-run efficiency. One natural formulation is the long-run reward per unit of time studied in Semi-Markov Decision Process (SMDP) ( Sutton et al., 1999b ; Das et al., 1999 ; György et al., 2007 ) . Intuitively, the method uses RL to maximize relative rewards, calculated from total rewards minus the amount that it would have earned if time were spent optimally. However, performing this computation requires knowing the optimal reward rate apriori , which is often not the case in practice, giving a chicken-or-egg dilemma. Existing approaches mainly use two ways to tackle this. Directly optimizing the reward rate with SMDP policy gradient objective ( Sutton et al., 1999a ) requires estimating the rate of the current policy from on-policy rollouts, an operation that is still expensive when actions are costly. The continuous-time bandit approach ( György et al., 2007 ) estimates the optimal reward rate from historical samples, but it requires an exhaustive search over the policy space, infeasible in modern agentic RL settings where action space is large. To that end, we propose Reward-rate Policy Gradient (RPG) , which uses off-policy historical samples to estimate the reward rate under the greedy policy and maximizes for relative reward ( Figure 1 ). RPG avoids the limitations of the two previous methods. It does not need time-costly on-policy rollouts for each gradient step, and does not require searching over the policy space. Additionally, RPG is simple to adopt in the current RL pipeline, since it only requires a reward-rate estimator and uses the relative reward as the learning signal. We first study RPG in the bandit setting and theoretically prove that, in expectation, if the greedy policy’s reward rate is estimated well, then RPG is equivalent to the Dinkelbach iteration ( Dinkelbach, 1967 ; Schaible, 1976 ) , and natural policy gradient (NPG) ( Amari, 1998 ) is suited for reward-rate optimization due to preconditioning on Fisher information. Experiments on the bandit setting confirm that RPG obtains lower regret than the reward-rate upper-confidence-bound algorithm by György et al. (2007) without the need to search over the policy space. These findings motivate us to apply Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) , a first-order approximation of NPG methods ( Kakade, 2001 ; Schulman et al., 2015 ) , on MLE-Bench and NanoGPT. Compared against vanilla RL baselines on the same time budget, RPG shows a 19.2% average improvement in performance across 20 out of 22 MLE-Bench tasks and an 85.7% margin on NanoGPT. Our findings demonstrate that RPG is a practical solution for future agentic RL frameworks where actions are costly.
